narrative: During the 2000s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continued to thrive, building upon the momentum of the natural hair movement that originated in the 1960s. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth or using chemical curling products, remained a staple, while cornrows, a traditional style of braiding practiced in many African cultures, became increasingly popular as a protective and stylish choice. Dreadlocks, also known as dreads or locs, gained popularity among some individuals, formed either naturally or through techniques like twisting or backcombing. As part of the natural hair movement, women began embracing their kinky hair texture, which was characterized by its density and kinked patterns. Box braids, a "protective style" that consisted of square-shaped hair divisions, also gained popularity among Black Africans and the African diaspora. While documentation from this era is limited in terms of specific hairstyles and trends popularized during the 2000s, it is clear that women were increasingly embracing their natural textures and exploring various protective styles to celebrate their identity and culture.
